issues.legal_issue: Heirs entitled to succeed to an owner’s property may claim it on the termination of a limited life interest, notwithstanding a gift made by the life-interest holder.
material_facts: The original owner’s widow inherited only a life interest in the suit property.

While holding that interest, she gifted the property to the defendant; the earlier court held the gift effective only during her lifetime and declared that it would not affect the reversionary rights after her death.
The plaintiffs, who were daughters of the original owner, sought possession on the basis of inheritance after the life-interest holder’s death.
The plaintiffs were not parties to the earlier suit and asserted their title independently of its declaratory decree.
issues.conclusion: The gift did not defeat the plaintiffs’ entitlement to inherit when the life interest ended; they could claim title and possession on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Hindu Succession Act, succession reopened on the death of the holder of a limited life interest, and the original owner’s daughters inherited his interest. A declaratory decree obtained by a reversioner does not bind the actual owner, though a decree concerning an alienation may remove an obstacle to the rights of those entitled when succession opens. The Court relied on Giasi Ram and Others v. Ramjilal and Others and Shankuntla Devi v. Kamla and Others.

rule.if: possession_suit_based_on_inheritance and prior_owner_had_only_life_interest and gift_effective_only_during_life and heirs_entitled_when_life_interest_ended

predicates.possession_suit_based_on_inheritance: The claimants brought a civil suit seeking possession on the basis that they inherited the property.
predicates.prior_owner_had_only_life_interest: The person who transferred the property held only a life interest in it.
predicates.gift_effective_only_during_life: The transfer was effective only for the lifetime of the limited-interest holder.
predicates.heirs_entitled_when_life_interest_ended: The claimants were entitled to succeed to the original owner’s interest when the life interest ended.

issues.definition: When a possession suit rests on inheritance and the transferor held only a life interest, heirs entitled to succeed when that interest ends may claim title and possession despite a transfer effective only during that lifetime.

issues.legal_issue: The limitation period for challenging a customary alienation of ancestral property does not govern a suit for possession based on inheritance where the plaintiffs’ title arises on the termination of a life interest.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought possession as heirs after the death of the holder of a life interest.
An earlier final decree had declared that the gift would not affect the reversionary rights arising after the life-interest holder’s death.
The plaintiffs’ claim was based on inherited title, rather than a fresh challenge to an alienation as contrary to custom.
issues.conclusion: The three-year limitation provision for a suit challenging an alienation of ancestral property under custom did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 2(b) of the Schedule to the Punjab Limitation (Customs) Act, 1920 applies to a suit for possession of ancestral immovable property alienated where the plaintiff asserts that the alienation is not binding under custom. It did not apply to a claim based on title already declared in an earlier suit and inheritance on the termination of a life interest.

predicates.possession_suit_based_on_inheritance: The claimants brought a civil suit seeking possession on the basis of inherited title.
predicates.claim_arises_when_life_interest_ends: The claimants’ entitlement arose when a limited life interest ended.
predicates.suit_challenges_alienation_as_customaril: The claimants sought possession on the ground that an alienation of ancestral property was invalid under custom.

issues.definition: A suit for inherited possession arising when a life interest ends is not governed by the customary-alienation limitation rule when it does not challenge an alienation as invalid under custom.

issues.legal_issue: A presumption of death arising from a person not being heard of for seven years does not establish the date on which that person died.
material_facts: The life-interest holder had not been heard of for more than seven years by people who would naturally have heard from her if she were alive.
Neither side proved her actual date of death.
The dispute involved the date of death, rather than whether she was presumed to be dead.
issues.conclusion: The court could presume that she was dead once the required seven-year absence had elapsed, but could not presume that she died at any particular time during that period or seven years before the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 107 and 108 of the Indian Evidence Act distinguish the presumption that a person is dead from proof of the time of death. The person asserting death at a particular time bears the burden of proving it. The Court relied on Lal Chand Marwari v. Mahant Ramrups Gir and LIC of India v. Anuradha.

predicates.civil_case_requires_determination_of_dea: A civil dispute requires the court to determine when a person died.
predicates.person_unheard_for_seven_years_by_those_: The person had not been heard of for at least seven years by people who would naturally have heard from the person if alive.
predicates.death_time_not_proved: No party proved the person’s death at a particular time.

issues.definition: When a civil case requires a death date, seven years of absence from the notice of those who would naturally hear from the person does not establish a particular date of death without further proof.

issues.legal_issue: In a suit for possession based on title, the defendant’s possession bars the claim through limitation only if the defendant establishes adverse possession, including the required intention to possess as owner.
material_facts: The plaintiffs established title to the property by inheritance.
The defendant did not plead that he had perfected title by adverse possession and stated that his possession was not adverse to the true owner.
The defendant did not intend to raise an adverse-possession plea before the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation because the plaintiffs had proved title and the defendant had not pleaded adverse possession; the burden to establish adverse possession rested on the defendant.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, limitation for possession based on title begins when the defendant’s possession becomes adverse, and the plaintiff need not prove possession within the preceding twelve years. A defendant relying on adverse possession must plead and prove the facts establishing it, including exclusive possession and animus possidendi. The Court relied on Vasantiben Prahladji Nayak v. Somnath Muljibhai Nayak, Md. Mohammad Ali v. Jagdish Kalita, and Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India.

rule.if: appeal_in_title_based_possession_suit and plaintiffs_proved_title and not defendant_pleaded_adverse_possession

predicates.appeal_in_title_based_possession_suit: The matter is an appeal in a suit seeking possession on the basis of title.
predicates.plaintiffs_proved_title: The claimants established their title to the property.
predicates.defendant_pleaded_adverse_possession: The defendant pleaded that possession had become adverse to the true owner and had perfected title by adverse possession.

issues.definition: In an appeal in a title-based possession suit, where the claimants prove title and the defendant does not plead adverse possession, the suit is not barred by limitation on that basis.
